City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team

Public Team And Project Profile

Research checked: October 8, 2026

Scope: Publicly available resources located online about the City of Edmonton’s Data Science and Research (DSR) team, publicly named members and collaborators, named projects, and the municipal context in which the team works. This is a source-based profile, not a complete staff directory or internal project register.

Overview

The City describes DSR as a team applying data science and artificial intelligence (AI) to operational municipal problems. Its public examples emphasize working with service-area staff and subject-matter experts, selecting methods that fit the decision, and planning for operational use rather than treating a model as a stand-alone research result. A 2025 presentation describes the group as a centralized team formed in 2020; a City article about WildEdmonton says it was founded in 2021. The sources may be describing different milestones, so the exact founding date is unclear.

The City article describes the team as having eight members at the time it was written, but it does not name them all. The 2025 Upper Bound session identifies four team presenters. Those four are the publicly named members that can be confidently associated with the team from the sources found here; this should not be read as a complete or current roster. A 2018 City data-science event identifies earlier contributors, shown separately below.

In September 2026, Taproot reported that the applied AI division had completed 77 projects and had 50 at different stages in its queue. Public coverage therefore documents only a fraction of the team’s work; the project list below is limited to initiatives for which a public source was found.

Earlier Publicly Identified Contributors

These names are associated with earlier City data-science work, not verified as current DSR staff:

  • Ben Gready — named as a City data scientist presenting on data-science projects at a 2018 event; later public coverage and a City safety-code FAQ associate him with the earlier AI-enabled safety-code inspection initiative.
  • Roman Eisner — named with Gready as a City data scientist presenting on data-science projects at the same 2018 event.

The 2018 event also included presenters and panelists from the City’s Smart City & Analytics Centre of Excellence. The available event page does not establish that all listed participants were DSR team members.

Publicly Documented Projects

Names, status, and level of attribution below follow the linked sources. “Current” indicates described as active or operational in the cited material, not independently verified as of the research date.

Project Purpose and public status People or partners linked in sources
Ember Wise / Amberwise Wildfire-risk monitoring and forecasting. The Upper Bound presentation describes use of weather, forest-fuel, and topographic information; a location-based risk component is operational, while use of calls-for-service data to explore behavior-related ignition risk was still in development. Amii’s session description spells the name “Amberwise”; the presentation notes use “Ember Wise.” Zehra Shah presented this work.
Residential safety-code inspection triage A model to help prioritize discretionary residential safety-code inspections. The 2025 talk stresses that mandatory inspections remain required and describes choosing error thresholds with inspectors and operational partners. Earlier City and award coverage describes the Safety Codes Inspection Efficiencies (SCIE) initiative; public sources do not establish that every historical and current model version is identical. Clayton Clemens presented the 2025 project. Ben Gready is associated with the earlier SCIE initiative.
Repair A map-based workflow for filtering and prioritizing pothole reports, with historical information and next-week pothole estimates by road zone. The Upper Bound talk says the team moved from trying to predict individual notifications to forecasting counts by zone because report descriptions and images were often missing. A voice-activated reporting app was shown as a prototype. Taher Abbasi presented the project.
WildEdmonton City–University of Alberta wildlife monitoring partnership, running since 2018. The City’s account says the DSR team built an AI-assisted image workflow using Microsoft’s CameraTraps MegaDetector to identify and filter images containing people, improving privacy and processing efficiency for wildlife research. City of Edmonton, University of Alberta, and DSR; the City identifies Clayton Clemens as a Senior Data Scientist involved in the work.
Unison Public-safety data and deployment tool that combines partner incident-demand information into a shared operating picture. Reporting describes Decide for forecasting areas of demand and Track for monitoring trends and interventions. Its stated approach includes data minimization and excluding sensitive attributes and crime data that could produce feedback loops. Kris Andreychuk is identified as an architect of the tool. Reporting names City and community partners.
Text Depot Internal search and analysis tool for municipal text records. The City of Edmonton GitHub repository describes a dashboard for searching and analyzing text stored in Elasticsearch. An Apolitical case study attributes the broader platform to DSR and describes its internal use. Attributed to the DSR team in the case study; the City maintains a public GitHub repository for the dashboard.
Exposure Earlier project that scraped online “body rub” listings to help outreach workers identify people who might need assistance. Andreychuk said the project was taken over by police and later ended after the source site shut down. Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; not a current DSR project.
Symbol Smart Image-detection application intended to identify hate symbols. Andreychuk described the project as stalling because the departments that could use it could not agree on ownership. Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; status described as unsuccessful/stalled.
Used-needle collection route optimization Route-optimization work for pickups from public bins. Andreychuk described learning that operational staff did not find the proposed routes useful; the public account does not document its eventual disposition. Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting.
Workforce-injury reduction A project described as upcoming in September 2026 reporting; no public project name, technical details, or assigned team members were provided in the source. No individuals identified in the source.

The City and partner sources also refer to broader AI and data-science work, but do not publish a complete list of the 77 reported completed projects or the 50 queued projects. The items above are the named initiatives substantiated in the sources collected here, not an exhaustive portfolio.

  • Alberta AI: “Open Data, Data Science and Digital Innovation at City of Edmonton” — 2018 event page listing Ben Gready and Roman Eisner as data-science presenters.

City Of Edmonton Context Resources

These City resources help explain the operating environment around municipal data, research, privacy, and public services. They are institutional context, not all DSR policies or team-specific procedures.

  • City of Edmonton Open Data — browse and download public City datasets.
  • City of Edmonton: Open Data — overview of the City’s open-data program, transparency commitments, and sharing safeguards.
  • Open Data Strategy — City strategy record on the Open Data Portal.
  • About Open Data at the City of Edmonton — portal overview.
  • International Open Data Charter — City’s open-data charter context.
  • A1477 Data and Information Management Policy — City-wide data and information management policy.
  • Generative AI Standard — City requirements for generative-AI use.
  • Privacy Impact Assessment Administrative Standard — City privacy-assessment requirements.
  • Access to Information and Protection of Privacy — City information-access and privacy information.
  • Wildland-Urban Interface Wildfire Risk Strategy — broader wildfire-planning context for Ember Wise.

Source Notes And Limitations

  • The 2025 Amii session names four presenters; the City-published WildEdmonton article says the team had eight members but does not name the other four. Neither source establishes the full present-day staffing roster.
  • Public accounts differ on whether the team was formed in 2020 or founded in 2021. Both claims are retained here rather than selecting one without evidence.
  • The wildfire project name appears as “Ember Wise” in the presentation materials and “Amberwise” in Amii’s session summary.
  • Project names, operating status, and member associations are limited to what the cited public sources state. Similar project labels do not by themselves prove that models described in different years are the same implementation.
  • Some project descriptions rely on reporting and partner case studies rather than a City project page. Links are included so readers can distinguish those accounts from City-published resources.
